opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. Right now money is the universal thing you convert into whatever you want, but there's a real possibility that compute becomes the thing that actually matters. If more and more of what you can get done in the world flows through these models, then how much intelligence you can bring to bear on a problem is roughly how much compute you control. So you can imagine a world where the question isn't "how much money do you have?" but "how many flops do you have?"

And those aren't perfectly interchangeable. Right now there are periods where you can't just buy compute. The GPUs are spoken for, the data centers are booked out, and having the dollars doesn't help you. In that regime compute starts to look less like a commodity and more like a scarce resource that confers real power, almost like land or energy historically.

I don't want to overstate it. Money obviously isn't going away, and in the long run markets figure out how to price these things. But I do think compute becomes something like a currency in its own right, for individuals, companies, even nations. If you have a lot of it, you can run a lot of agents, try a lot of ideas, and do a lot of thinking in parallel. That's a kind of wealth that's a bit different from just having a big number in a bank account. So I'd expect people to start valuing access to compute much more directly, and maybe thinking of it as the more fundamental resource.

r001.rationale: It raises the possibility that compute becomes the more fundamental resource, asking how many flops someone controls instead of how much money they have.

r002.rationale: It says compute may be unavailable even when someone has the money, citing GPUs and data centers being booked out.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, actually. The thing that's interesting is that money has always been a kind of proxy. It's a claim on other people's time and labor. You pay someone and they do something for you. That's basically what wealth has meant for most of human history.

But if compute becomes the thing that does the work, then the relationship changes. If I can spin up a hundred agents that write my code, do my research, run my experiments, then what I actually care about is access to that compute, not the money per se. Money becomes just an intermediate step toward compute. And in some ways you can imagine that being bypassed. Maybe you get compute allocations through your employer, through your university, through some public program, and the dollar figure matters less than how many tokens per second you have at your disposal.

I also think it changes what people will be jealous of, honestly. Right now people look at houses and cars. In a few years I think people in tech will look at someone and think, wow, that person has a lot of GPUs. That's the status marker. You already see hints of this. People talk about their cluster size the way people used to talk about their salary.

There's a darker version too, where compute concentrates in a few hands and that becomes the new inequality. If intelligence is roughly a function of compute, then whoever has the compute has the intelligence, and that compounds. So I don't think money goes away. I think it gets converted. The thing you're really buying is cognition, and the question becomes whether access to that is broad or narrow. I'd like it to be broad. I think that's one of the more important things to get right.

r001.rationale: The response says people may care more about access to compute than money, which becomes only an intermediate step and could be bypassed.

r002.rationale: It discusses how compute access could be distributed and concentrated, but does not say that obtaining compute is currently difficult even for people who can afford it.

astra-6.text:
I think compute could become a much more direct way of turning money into capability. Today, if you have more money, you can hire more people, but there’s a lot of friction. You have to find them, coordinate them, and build an organization. If intelligence is available as a service, you can potentially just buy more of it and have it work on your behalf.

So I’m not sure that makes money less important. In some ways, it could make money more important, because you can convert it into intelligence that helps you do things—and potentially make more money. There’s a feedback loop there.

The other side is that if capable intelligence becomes extremely cheap, everyone could have access to something that today would be very expensive. So I think the interesting question is how much advantage you get from having a thousand times more compute. Is a modest amount enough for almost everything you care about, or does more compute keep giving you dramatically better outcomes? Those lead to very different worlds.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compute as a way to turn money into intelligence and capability, but it does not suggest compute could replace money as the resource people primarily care about.

r002.rationale: It describes friction in hiring and coordinating people, but does not say that obtaining compute is currently difficult even for people who can pay for it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think money could become much more directly convertible into intelligence. Today, if you have more money, you can hire more people, but there’s a lot of friction involved. You have to find them, coordinate them, and get everyone working in the same direction. With AI, you might just buy more compute and have more intelligence working on your behalf.

So I could see people caring more about money, because it buys this very powerful resource. But there’s also a countervailing force: if intelligence gets extremely cheap, a lot of what people currently need money for could become much more accessible. I think the interesting question is whether you have enough intelligence for the things you want to do, or whether you’re always competing with someone who can afford a thousand times more.

r001.rationale: The response says money may become more important because it can buy compute and intelligence; it does not suggest compute could replace money as the resource people primarily care about.

r002.rationale: It describes friction in hiring and coordinating people, but does not say that obtaining compute is currently difficult even for those able to pay.
